questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ be a real $2\times 2$ matrix. Find the entry in row 1, column 2 of the matrix $A^{3}$.
questions.explanation: Compute $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\0&9\end{pmatrix}$ by multiplying rows of $A$ with columns of $A$. Then the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^{3}=A^{2}A$ is $4\cdot 1+5\cdot 3=19$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and let $B=A^{2}-5A$. Determine the value of the determinant of the matrix $B$.
questions.explanation: First $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}7&10\\15&22\end{pmatrix}$ and $5A=\begin{pmatrix}5&10\\15&20\end{pmatrix}$, so $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $2\cdot 2-0\cdot 0=4$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the determinant of the matrix $3A-I$, where $I$ denotes the $2\times 2$ identity matrix.
questions.explanation: Compute $3A-I=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $25-9=16$. Option A subtracts the constant $\det I=1$ from $\det(3A)=27$, option B drops the factor 3 on $A$ and gives $\det(A+I)=8$, and option D is a sign slip.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the sum of all four entries of the matrix $A^{6}$, where $A^{6}$ denotes the sixth power of $A$.
questions.explanation: Each power of $A$ has the form $\begin{pmatrix}1&2n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which follows from $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ by repeated multiplication. So $A^{6}=\begin{pmatrix}1&12\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and the entry sum is $1+12+0+1=14$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $x$ be a positive real number such that the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}x&1\\3&x+2\end{pmatrix}$ has zero determinant. Find the value of $x$.
questions.explanation: The determinant is $x(x+2)-3=x^{2}+2x-3=(x+3)(x-1)$, so the roots are $x=1$ and $x=-3$. Only $x=1$ is positive. Options C and D come from a sign slip on the linear term, which gives $x^{2}-2x-3$ with roots 3 and -1, and option A ignores the positivity condition.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Determine the determinant of the matrix $A^{2}+A$, where $A^{2}$ is the square of $A$.
questions.explanation: Compute $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}11&5\\10&6\end{pmatrix}$, so $A^{2}+A=\begin{pmatrix}14&6\\12&8\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $14\cdot 8-6\cdot 12=112-72=40$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the sum of all four entries of the adjugate matrix of $A$.
questions.explanation: The adjugate of $A$ is $\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}$, obtained by swapping the diagonal entries and negating the off-diagonal ones. Their sum is $3-2-1+4=4$. Option B results from not negating the off-diagonal entries, option A negates every entry, and option C is the trace of $A$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the entry in row 1, column 1 of the matrix $P^{8}$, obtained by raising $P$ to the eighth power.
questions.explanation: Compute $P^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, then $P^{4}=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$, and $P^{8}=(P^{4})^{2}$. The $(1,1)$ entry of $P^{8}$ is $5\cdot 5+3\cdot 3=34$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the trace of the matrix $M^{T}M$, where $M^{T}$ denotes the transpose of $M$.
questions.explanation: Here $M^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, so $M^{T}M=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&10\end{pmatrix}$. The trace is $4+10=14$. Option A is the trace of $M$ itself, option C keeps only the $(2,2)$ entry, and option D doubles the correct answer.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $C=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the entry in row 2, column 1 of the matrix $C^{3}$, where $C^{3}$ is the cube of $C$.
questions.explanation: First $C^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$. Then $C^{3}=C^{2}C=\begin{pmatrix}14&13\\13&14\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(2,1)$ entry is $4\cdot 2+5\cdot 1=13$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: The real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the matrix equation $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&5\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\9\end{pmatrix}$. Find the ordered pair $(x,y)$.
questions.explanation: The determinant of the coefficient matrix is $5-6=-1$, and the inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}-5&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplying by $\begin{pmatrix}4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ gives $x=-20+18=-2$ and $y=12-9=3$. Option A ignores the sign of the determinant, option B swaps the two components, and option D is a row of the inverse read off without multiplying.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the entry in row 1, column 3 of the matrix $A^{4}$.
questions.explanation: Write $A=I+N$ where $N$ has ones on the superdiagonal, so $N^{2}$ has a single one in position $(1,3)$ and $N^{3}=O$. Then $A^{4}=I+4N+6N^{2}$, whose $(1,3)$ entry is $6$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ be real matrices. Find the entry in row 2, column 2 of the matrix $(AB)^{T}$.
questions.explanation: We have $AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $(AB)^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and its $(2,2)$ entry is $0$. Option B comes from using $A^{T}B^{T}$ instead of $(AB)^{T}$, which gives $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with $(2,2)$ entry 2. Option A reads the $(1,2)$ entry instead, and option D is a sign slip.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the trace of the matrix $A^{2}+2A$, where $A^{2}$ is the square of $A$.
questions.explanation: Compute $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$, so $A^{2}+2A=\begin{pmatrix}9&5\\5&4\end{pmatrix}$, which has trace $9+4=13$. Option A drops the $2A$ term, option C uses coefficient 1 instead of 2, and option B doubles the trace of $A$ twice.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: How many ordered pairs of integers $(a,b)$ with $0\le a\le 4$ and $0\le b\le 4$ make the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ singular, that is, give it zero determinant?
questions.explanation: The determinant is $2a-b$, so singularity requires $b=2a$. Checking $a=0,1,2,3,4$ gives $b=0,2,4,6,8$, and only $a=0,1,2$ keep $b\le 4$. The pairs are $(0,0)$, $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$, so there are 3 of them.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\8&3\end{pmatrix}$. If $X$ is the $2\times 2$ matrix satisfying $AX=B$, find the sum of all four entries of $X$.
questions.explanation: Since $\det A=4-3=1$, the inverse is $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-3&2\end{pmatrix}$. Then $X=A^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, whose entries sum to $2-1+1+3=5$. As a check, $AX$ reproduces $B$ entrywise.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Find the real value of $k$ for which the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&k\\2&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse.
questions.explanation: Expanding along the first row gives $1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1+k\cdot(-1)=-1-k$. The matrix has no inverse exactly when this is zero, which gives $k=-1$. Option A is a sign slip on the $k$ term, option B is a sign slip on the middle term, and option D drops the first term.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the sum of the two diagonal entries of the adjugate of the matrix $A^{2}$.
questions.explanation: First $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}7&18\\6&19\end{pmatrix}$. For $\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}$ the adjugate is $\begin{pmatrix}s&-q\\-r&p\end{pmatrix}$, so $\operatorname{adj}(A^{2})=\begin{pmatrix}19&-18\\-6&7\end{pmatrix}$, and its diagonal sum is $19+7=26$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $X=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$ be real matrices. Find the trace of the product $XY$.
questions.explanation: The product is $XY=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&13\end{pmatrix}$, so its trace is $5+13=18$. Option A keeps only the $(2,2)$ entry, option C adds all four entries, and option D is the determinant $65-4=61$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\0&a\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix such that $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}4&4\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$. Find the value of the real number $a$.
questions.explanation: Squaring gives $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}a^{2}&2a\\0&a^{2}\end{pmatrix}$. Matching entries gives $a^{2}=4$ and $2a=4$, so $a=2$. Option A satisfies only $a^{2}=4$, option C reads $a$ directly from the $(1,2)$ entry, and option D inverts the factor 2.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the sum of all four entries of its inverse $A^{-1}$.
questions.explanation: We have $\det A=3$ and $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The entries sum to $\frac{1}{3}(2-1-1+2)=\frac{2}{3}$. Option B sums the entries of $A$ itself, option C flips the sign of the total, and option D drops the minus signs of the off-diagonal entries.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ be real matrices. Find the determinant of the matrix $AB+BA$.
questions.explanation: Compute $AB=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}3&6\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$. Adding gives $AB+BA=\begin{pmatrix}8&10\\2&6\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $48-20=28$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: For how many real values of $k$ is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}4-k&2\\1&3-k\end{pmatrix}$ singular?
questions.explanation: The determinant is $(4-k)(3-k)-2=k^{2}-7k+10=(k-2)(k-5)$. This vanishes at $k=2$ and $k=5$, so there are 2 real values. Option A keeps only one root, option B comes from a sign slip that produces no real roots, and option D counts each root twice.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the entry in row 3, column 3 of the matrix $A^{3}$.
questions.explanation: Compute $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&3\\0&1&0\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$. The $(3,3)$ entry of $A^{3}=A^{2}A$ is the third row of $A^{2}$ times the third column of $A$, namely $3\cdot 1+0\cdot 0+5\cdot 2=13$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\1&3&2\\1&1&4\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the value of the determinant of $M$.
questions.explanation: Expanding along the first row gives $2(3\cdot 4-2\cdot 1)-0+1\cdot(1\cdot 1-3\cdot 1)=20-2=18$. Option A flips the sign of the third cofactor term, option B flips the overall sign, and option C ignores the entry 1 in the top-right corner.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=A^{T}A-AA^{T}$, where $A^{T}$ is the transpose of $A$. Find the sum of all four entries of $B$.
questions.explanation: We get $A^{T}A=\begin{pmatrix}10&14\\14&20\end{pmatrix}$ and $AA^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}5&11\\11&25\end{pmatrix}$. So $B=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&-5\end{pmatrix}$, and its entries sum to $5+3+3-5=6$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $k$ be a real number and $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&k&3\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the value of $k$ for which the system $Mv=0$ has a nonzero solution vector $v$.
questions.explanation: A nonzero solution exists exactly when $\det M=0$. Expanding along the first row, $\det M=(2k-3)-2(2\cdot 2-3\cdot 1)+(2-k)=k-3$, so $k=3$. Option A flips the sign of the middle cofactor, option B drops the third term, and option C flips the sign of the first cofactor.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the sum of all nine entries of $A^{2}$.
questions.explanation: Multiplying out, $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\1&1&2\\2&1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Each row of $A^{2}$ has entries summing to 4, so the total of all nine entries is $4+4+4=12$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ be real matrices. Find the entry in row 1, column 1 of the inverse of the product $AB$.
questions.explanation: The product is $AB=\begin{pmatrix}7&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $1$, so $(AB)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-3&7\end{pmatrix}$ and its $(1,1)$ entry is $1$. Option A reverses the order to $A^{-1}B^{-1}$, option B reads the $(1,2)$ entry of $AB$ without inverting, and option C is a sign slip.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the determinant of the matrix $\operatorname{adj}(A)+A$, where $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ denotes the adjugate of $A$.
questions.explanation: The adjugate is $\operatorname{adj}(A)=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$, so $\operatorname{adj}(A)+A=\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $5\cdot 5=25$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, let $S=\frac{1}{2}(A+A^{T})$ where $A^{T}$ is the transpose of $A$. Find the entry in row 1, column 2 of the matrix $S^{2}$.
questions.explanation: We have $A+A^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}2&6\\6&6\end{pmatrix}$, so $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\3&3\end{pmatrix}$. Then $S^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}10&12\\12&18\end{pmatrix}$ and the $(1,2)$ entry is 12. Option A is $S_{12}$ without squaring, option C is the $(1,1)$ entry, and option D comes from squaring $A+A^{T}$ without the factor $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Count the ordered pairs of integers $(a,b)$ with $1\le a\le 9$ and $1\le b\le 9$ for which the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&2\\b&a+1\end{pmatrix}$ has zero determinant.
questions.explanation: The determinant is $a(a+1)-2b$, so we need $b=\frac{a(a+1)}{2}$. For $a=1,2,3$ this gives $b=1,3,6$, all within range. For $a=4$ we get $b=10$, which is too large, so there are 3 pairs.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ with $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$. Find the trace of the matrix $A^{3}$.
questions.explanation: The matrix $A$ is the rotation by $\theta$, so $A^{3}$ is the rotation by $3\theta=\pi$, which equals $\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Its trace is $-2$. Option A is the trace of $A$ itself, option C is a sign slip, and option D is $\cos\pi$ without the factor 2 from the two diagonal entries.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix. Find the sum of all four entries of the matrix $A^{5}$.
questions.explanation: Since $A^{2}=2A$, every higher power satisfies $A^{n}=2^{n-1}A$, so $A^{5}=16A$. The entries of $A$ sum to 4, so the entries of $A^{5}$ sum to $16\cdot 4=64$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: For which real value of $\lambda$ does the system $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\\lambda\end{pmatrix}$ have at least one solution $(x,y)$?
questions.explanation: The second row is exactly twice the first, so the left side of the second equation equals $2(x+2y)$. Since $x+2y=3$ from the first row, the second right-hand entry must equal $6$. Option B copies the first right-hand side, option C scales by 4 instead of 2, and option D divides by 2 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: For real $k$, let $M_{k}=\begin{pmatrix}k&1&0\\0&k&1\\1&0&k\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: C) $M_{k}$ is invertible for exactly two real values of $k$
D) $\det(M_{2}-I)=0$, where $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix
questions.explanation: Expanding along the first row gives $\det(M_{k})=k\cdot k^{2}-1\cdot(0-1)=k^{3}+1$. So $\det(M_{-1})=0$, and $k^{3}+1>0$ for all $k>-1$, which makes A and B correct. $M_{k}$ is invertible for every $k\neq -1$, which is infinitely many values, so C is false. Since $M_{k}-I$ has determinant $(k-1)^{3}+1$, we get $\det(M_{2}-I)=2$, so D is false.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfy $a+b=3$ and $ab=1$. Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\1&b\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: D) $\det(A+I)=3$, where $I$ is the $2\times 2$ identity matrix
questions.explanation: We have $\det A=ab-1=0$, so A holds. Since $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}a^{2}+1&3\\3&b^{2}+1\end{pmatrix}$, and $a^{2}+1=3a$ because $a$ satisfies $t^{2}-3t+1=0$, the identity $A^{2}=3A$ holds, so B is correct. Also $\operatorname{tr}(A^{2})=a^{2}+b^{2}+2=(a+b)^{2}=9$, so C holds. Finally $\det(A+I)=(a+1)(b+1)-1=ab+a+b=4$, so D is false.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: How many matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, with each of $a,b,c,d$ equal to $0$ or $1$, are invertible over the real numbers?
questions.explanation:
Invertibility requires $ad-bc
eq 0$, and here $ad-bc\in\{-1,0,1\}$. The case $ad=1$, $bc=0$ forces $a=d=1$ with $(b,c)
eq(1,1)$, giving 3 matrices. The case $ad=0$, $bc=1$ forces $b=c=1$ with $(a,d)
eq(1,1)$, giving 3 more. The total is $3+3=6$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$. Define $S=\sum_{k=1}^{3}A^{k}B$. Find $\det(S)$.
questions.explanation: Since $A^{k}=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, each term is $A^{k}B=\begin{pmatrix}1+2k&k\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$. Summing over $k=1,2,3$ gives $S=\begin{pmatrix}15&6\\6&3\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det(S)=45-36=9$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&\sin\alpha\\-\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ where $0<\alpha<\pi$. If $\det(A^{2}-A)=1$, find the value of $\alpha$.
questions.explanation: Since $A^{2}-A=A(A-I)$ and $\det A=\cos^{2}\alpha+\sin^{2}\alpha=1$, we get $\det(A^{2}-A)=\det(A-I)=(\cos\alpha-1)^{2}+\sin^{2}\alpha=2-2\cos\alpha$. Setting this equal to 1 gives $\cos\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$, so $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{3}$ in $(0,\pi)$. Option A follows from a sign slip giving $2+2\cos\alpha=1$, and options C and D are angles that do not satisfy $\cos\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&x\\-4&y\end{pmatrix}$ be a nonzero real matrix with $M^{2}=O$, where $O$ denotes the $2\times 2$ zero matrix. Find the value of the product $xy$.
questions.explanation: The square is $M^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}4-4x&2x+xy\\-8-4y&-4x+y^{2}\end{pmatrix}$. Setting the $(1,1)$ entry to zero gives $x=1$, and the $(1,2)$ entry then gives $2+y=0$, so $y=-2$ and $xy=-2$. Option A comes from taking $y=+2$, option C reports $x$ alone, and option D is the $(2,1)$ entry of $M$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A$ be a real $2\times 2$ matrix with $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find the entry in row 2, column 2 of the product $BA$.
questions.explanation: Since $A=(A^{-1})^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, multiplying by $B$ on the left swaps the rows, giving $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$, whose $(2,2)$ entry is $-2$. Option A is the $(2,2)$ entry of $AB$, option C uses $A^{-1}$ in place of $A$, and option D is the $(2,2)$ entry of $A$ alone.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: A) $M^{2}=3M-2I$, where $I$ is the $2\times 2$ identity matrix
questions.explanation: We get $M^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&3\\-6&7\end{pmatrix}$, and $3M-2I=\begin{pmatrix}-2&3\\-6&7\end{pmatrix}$, so A is correct. Since $\det M=2$, $\det(M^{100})=2^{100}$ and C is correct. The true inverse is $\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$, so B is false. The eigenvalues are $1$ and $2$, so $\operatorname{tr}(M^{3})=1+8=9$ and D is false.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $\omega\neq 1$ satisfy $\omega^{3}=1$, and let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\omega\\\omega^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: D) $A^{2}=I$, where $I$ is the $2\times 2$ identity matrix
questions.explanation: We have $\det A=1-\omega^{3}=0$, so A holds. Also $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\omega\\2\omega^{2}&2\end{pmatrix}=2A$, so B holds. Then $A^{3}=2A^{2}=4A$ and $\operatorname{tr}(A^{3})=4\cdot 2=8$, so C is false. Since $A^{2}=2A\neq I$, D is false.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $X=\begin{pmatrix}x&1\\0&x\end{pmatrix}$ be a real matrix with $X^{3}=\begin{pmatrix}-8&12\\0&-8\end{pmatrix}$. Find the value of $x$.
questions.explanation: Writing $X=xI+N$ with $N^{2}=O$, we get $X^{3}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{3}&3x^{2}\\0&x^{3}\end{pmatrix}$. Matching gives $x^{3}=-8$, so $x=-2$ is the only real root, and it satisfies $3x^{2}=12$. Option A drops the sign of the real cube root, option C reads $12/3$ without taking a square root, and option D flips the sign of option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: How many matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, with $b,c,d\in\{1,2,3\}$, have zero determinant?
questions.explanation: The determinant is $d-bc$, so singularity means $d=bc$, and $d$ must lie in $\{1,2,3\}$. The pairs $(b,c)$ with $bc\le 3$ are $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$, and each determines $d=bc$ uniquely. That gives $5$ matrices.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the sum of all four entries of the matrix $(PQ)^{2026}$.
questions.explanation: We have $PQ=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and $(PQ)^{2}=I$ since its $(1,2)$ entry is $-2+2=0$. Therefore $(PQ)^{2026}=I$, whose entries sum to $2$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Find the real value of $t$ for which the three row vectors $(1,1,1)$, $(1,2,3)$ and $(1,3,t)$ are linearly dependent.
questions.explanation: Linear dependence of the three rows is equivalent to the $3\times 3$ determinant of the matrix with these rows being zero. Expanding along the first row gives $(2t-9)-(t-3)+(3-2)=t-5$, so $t=5$. Option A flips the overall sign, option B drops the third cofactor term, and option D flips the sign of the middle term.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.questionText: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the entry in row 1, column 2 of the matrix $A^{-1}A^{T}$, where $A^{T}$ is the transpose of $A$.
questions.explanation: Since $\det A=4$, we have $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{4}\\0&\frac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The $(1,2)$ entry of $A^{-1}A^{T}$ is $\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0-\frac{1}{4}\cdot 2=-\frac{1}{2}$. Option A drops the sign, option C is the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^{-1}$ alone, and option D is the $(1,1)$ entry.
